classification.text_en: The Quran speaks of an ant (namlah) and of the ants (al-naml) as a group with a valley and dwellings.

origin.note_en: The Quran does not describe the creation of the ant in particular.

purpose.note_en: The Quran does not state a purpose for the ant.

nature.text_en: The ants are shown as a group with dwellings, addressed by one of their number.

abilities.text_en: One ant speaks to the others, tells them to enter their dwellings and names the risk that Sulayman and his soldiers might crush them without perceiving it.

limitations.note_en: The Quran does not describe limits of the ants themselves.

relationship_with_humans.text_en: Sulayman, passing with his hosts, smiled laughing at the ant's words and prayed to be inspired to thank God for His favour on him and on his parents.

quranic_events.text_en: Sulayman's hosts of jinn, men and birds were gathered and kept in ranks. When they came to the valley of the ants, one ant spoke, and Sulayman smiled and prayed.

chronological_position.text_en: The event is set in Sulayman's time, after he inherited from Dawud. The passage gives no date.

location.text_en: The place is the valley of the ants.

misconceptions.text_en: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the verse reports what the ant said and that Sulayman smiled. It does not describe how ants communicate in general, and this profile adds nothing about that.

lessons.text_en: Educational interpretation (not scripture): the verse sets an ant's warning to its fellows beside a king's prayer of thanks, and it is read as a lesson in care for others and in gratitude.

vocabulary.text_en: Words used: al-naml (the ants), namlah (an ant), wad al-naml (the valley of the ants), masakinakum (your dwellings), yahtimannakum (crush you).
